newsitem.title: USA: Wall Street open hinges on July employment data.
newsitem.headline: Wall Street open hinges on July employment data.

text.p: Wall Street shares should take their opening cues from the July payrolls data, stumbling if the data raised fears of excessive economic growth but rising if the numbers came in as forecast, analysts said.

In addition to the employment data, due at 0830 EDT/1230 GMT, stocks and bonds would also face the July National Association of Purchasing Managers (NAPM) index at 1000 EDT/1400 GMT. This will be watched for inflation signals.

"The employment data is the first significant third quarter number," Pierre Ellis, senior economist at Primark Decision Economics, said. "Depending on what the data indicates, people will form broad impressions about third quarter growth."
Larry Wachtel, an analyst at Prudential Securities, said: "The employment number is very important. Depending on how that comes in, we will have a call on the open."
Economists surveyed by Reuters forecast nonfarm payrolls would rise by 193,000 versus a previous gain of 217,000 jobs. The unemployment rate was seen dipping to 4.9 percent.
Average hourly earnings were expected to rise 0.2 percent from a rise of 0.3 percent in June, and the average work week was forecast to decline to 34.6 hours.
Ellis said a sharp jump in nonfarm payrolls, coupled with a longer work week, would create concern about powerful third quarter growth and inflation.
"The unemployement rate also has to be watched carefully because it is so low," he said.
After the employment data, markets will face the July NAPM data, searching for signs of upward pressure on prices.
The NAPM index was expected to read 56.1 in July compared to 55.7 in June.
But analysts said the prices paid component would attract more attention, after the Chicago PMI data released yesterday showed a rise in input prices and sent bonds and stocks lower.
Other economic due on Friday included June personal income and consumption figures and factory orders.
Ahead of the data, the Standard & Poor's futures index was off 0.45 points at 957.50. The long bond was up 6/32 to yield 6.29 percent.
The dollar recouped earlier losses against the yen in Tokyo, as U.S. funds bought. It was trading at 118.85/95 yen. In Europe, the dollar was trading at 1.8472/82 marks.
Japan's Nikkei average closed off 527.05 points, or 2.59 percent, at 19,804.38.
Tokyo stocks slumped after a technical glitch, which halted electronic system trades on the Tokyo bourse in the morning, caused arbitrage-linked sales when trading resumed.
In London, the FTSE 100 was up 22.2 at 4929.7.
U.S. stocks were stagnant in light London trading, awaiting the economic data.

The Wall Street Journal said in its Heard on the Street column that for now, investors are betting Internet bookseller Amazon.com Inc will maintain its lead over rival booksellers, but there could be more on-line competion ahead.

The New York Times said in its Market Place column that some large U.S. financial firms are trying to block a proposed new accounting rule which would require companies to show derivative securities on their balance sheets.
((Wall Street desk 212-859=1730))
